svg.aria-label: Diagram: what an Amazon Verified Permissions authorization response actually contains, what the policy store schema does and does not constrain, and what an identifier inside a Cedar policy refers to over time. Verified Permissions currently uses Cedar version 4.7. For the IsAuthorized operation the caller must submit principal, action, resource, context and entities elements, and Verified Permissions evaluates the request against all policies in the requested policy store that apply to the entities in the request, where the entities element is the slice of application data supplied so that Cedar has something to reason over. A policy is a statement that either permits or forbids a principal to take one or more actions on a resource, and each policy is evaluated independently of every other policy, so there is no ordering, precedence numbering or inheritance and the combination rules are the whole of the arbitration. A successful call returns HTTP 200 and three response elements that matter. The decision element indicates whether the request should be allowed or denied, with valid values ALLOW and DENY. The determiningPolicies element is the list of determining policies used to make the decision, and it distinguishes three situations that all reduce to the same decision word: where two matching policies conflict, one a forbid and one a permit, the forbid policy will be the determining policy, meaning somebody wrote a rule against the request; where multiple matching permit policies exist there would be multiple determining policies; and in the case that no policies match, and hence the response is DENY, there would be no determining policies, meaning nobody granted access and nobody forbade it either. An empty determining-policies array therefore means that no policy determined the decision, which is not the same as proving that no policy matched, because an applicable policy that fails during evaluation also determines nothing; the errors array is what distinguishes an ordinary default denial from an evaluation failure, and the three outcomes belong in different queues. The errors element carries errors that occurred while making an authorization decision, for example a policy referencing an Entity or entity Attribute that does not exist in the slice; because errors arrive inside a successful 200 response rather than as a call failure, a permit policy that references an attribute the request did not supply produces an error entry, does not contribute to the decision, and the caller receives a well-formed DENY, so a non-empty errors array should be treated as an alarm rather than as diagnostics, its practical shape being that somebody adds an attribute condition to a permit policy, the application is not updated to pass that attribute, and access quietly stops working. On the schema, a schema is a declaration of the structure of the entity types supported by the application and the actions the application may provide in authorization requests, and its use in Verified Permissions is optional though highly recommended for production software. Policy validation mode controls whether policy changes are validated against the schema: when validation is turned on, all attempts to create or update a policy or policy template are validated against the schema and Verified Permissions rejects the request attempt if validation fails, and if validation is activated then all new policies must conform with the schema. The console offers Strict, which is recommended, or Off, and turning it off requires typing the word confirm to acknowledge that updates to policies will no longer be validated against the schema, while the same change can be made through the UpdatePolicyStore operation by specifying a different value for the ValidationSettings parameter, so the guardrail exists in one interface only and the control that actually binds is a policy on that API call rather than the console prompt. AWS recommends leaving validation off during application development and turning it on for testing and leaving it on in production. The consequence, and a correction to what the preceding post in this series promised, is that the schema constrains policy authoring at write time rather than constraining authorization at decision time: it is optional, it is gated by a mode that AWS suggests starting in the off position, it applies to new policies rather than retroactively revalidating those already stored, and it is not consulted when a decision is made, which means policies written during development while validation was off are the ones that have not been checked against it, and will not be until something edits them. On identifiers, AWS warns that if a user named jane leaves the company and someone else is later allowed to use the name jane, the new user automatically gets access to everything granted by policies that still reference User colon colon jane, because Cedar cannot distinguish between the new user and the old; AWS therefore strongly recommends universally unique identifiers for all principal and resource identifiers, identifiers that are guaranteed unique and never reused, and notes explicitly that this applies to both principal and resource identifiers, so a recycled document reference inherits the permissions written for whatever previously held it. AWS also advises against including personally identifying, confidential or sensitive information in these identifiers because they are included in log entries shared in AWS CloudTrail trails, and suggests following a UUID with a double-slash comment naming the entity to keep policies legible to a human. Policy names, by contrast, must be unique for all policies within the policy store and are prefixed with name slash, so the system enforces uniqueness for the thing it owns and asks the customer to enforce it for the thing they own. Finally, the token-based operations tie this post to its predecessor: IsAuthorizedWithToken generates an authorization request from user data in JSON web tokens and populates all attributes to the principal from the claims in the user's ID or access token, and group or user principal type information cannot be included in such a request so all principal data must be populated into the JWT provided, which means the authorization decision is made from attributes that were true when the token was signed and the staleness window is the token lifetime. BatchIsAuthorized groups requests into a single batch operation that minimizes quota usage and returns decisions for each of up to 30 complex nested actions, which sets a ceiling on how many independently authorised elements one screen can carry per call.
svg.title: Three fields come back from an authorization call; reducing them to one is where the information is lost
svg.text: A DENY, an explicit forbid, and a policy that failed to evaluate look the same.
Amazon Verified Permissions — Cedar 4.7. What the response contains, and what the schema does not constrain.
What you assemble — and the one word carrying the weight
IsAuthorized( principal, action, resource, context, entities )
entities is the slice of your data you chose to send. Authorisation quality is bounded by it — and the errors
field exists precisely because a policy can reference something the slice does not contain.
HTTP 200 — and three fields come back. Most call sites keep one.
decision
“Valid Values: ALLOW | DENY”
The easy half of the answer, and
usually the whole of what is kept.
determiningPolicies
forbid + permit both match →
“the forbid policy will be the
determining policy”
several permits → several entries
no policies match → DENY, and
“no determining policies”
errors
“a policy references an Entity or
entity Attribute that does not exist
in the slice”
Arrives inside the 200, not as a
failure. The policy did not vote.
Alarm on it. It is not diagnostics.
An empty array means no policy decided — read errors to find out why
A forbid is a control working. Empty with no errors is usually a policy never written. Empty with errors is a
policy that meant to grant access and could not run. Three incidents, different queues, one word.
The arbitration is the whole model
“Each policy is evaluated independently of every
other policy.” No order, no precedence, no inheritance.
Batch is a quota feature, and a ceiling
“minimizes quota usage” · up to 30 actions per call.
Thirty buttons is one call — and sets a screen’s budget.
The schema constrains authoring, not authorisation — four qualifications, each narrowing it
“The use of schemas in Verified Permissions is optional” → it may not exist at all
validation mode is Strict or Off → it does nothing unless set
“all attempts to create or update a policy” are validated → it is a check on writes
“then all new policies must conform with the schema” → the stored ones are never re-checked
And AWS recommends “leaving validation off while you’re developing” — so the policies written then are the ones never checked.
And the identifier in a policy is just a string
“if user jane leaves the company, and you later let someone else use the name jane, then that new user automatically
gets access to everything granted by policies that still reference User::"jane". Cedar can’t distinguish between
the new user and the old.” — and AWS adds: “This applies to both principal and resource identifiers.”
UUIDs, never reused, with a // comment for legibility — and nothing personal in them, because identifiers are “included in log
entries shared in AWS CloudTrail trails”. An email address as a principal id fails both tests at once.
